The optimizer, an extension of the digital twin model, is tested against operational constraints of oil and water production to recommend ICV positions with projected flow rates and water cuts for each layer. Our findings align closely with a physics-based simulator, validating the approach within a 10% error range. This entire digital twin workflow helps provide a consistent and reliable well monitoring mechanism for the well along with reliable recommendations for production optimization decisions. The novelty in this approach is to provide accurate real-time flowrate estimates of complex multilateral/multilayer wells with intelligent completions. The digital twin workflow provides virtual sensing that helps estimate downhole well conditions with great reliability for production management and optimization.

records.title: Development of a Geological Hydrogen Storage Simulator For Cyclic Injection and Withdrawal Processes: Coupled Flow and Geomechanics With Capillary Hysteresis
records.summary: Abstract We have developed a high-fidelity, coupled flow and geomechanics simulator specifically designed for geological hydrogen storage. This simulator integrates non-isothermal multiphase multicomponent flow of hydrogen and water with geomechanics, accounting for elastoplastic behavior such as Mohr-Coulomb failure, essential for maintaining the geomechanical integrity of storage reservoirs. Additionally, the simulator addresses capillary hysteresis resulting from repeated drainage and imbibition cycles induced by periodic hydrogen injection and production. To model capillary hysteresis robustly, we employ a thermodynamically consistent return mapping algorithm utilizing the van Genuchten model for the capillary pressure curve. The coupling between flow and geomechanics is achieved through the fixed-stress sequential method. We validated our simulator using three test cases (1D, 2D, and 3D) to assess its numerical stability and capabilities. In the 1D case, we evaluated numerical stability during repeated hydrogen injection and production, where both capillary hysteresis and geomechanical failure occur simultaneously. The results demonstrated stability, accurately capturing Mohr-Coulomb failure and capillary hysteresis curves. For the 2D and 3D cases, which focused on wellbore integrity and field-scale simulation, respectively, the simulator consistently provided reasonable and stable results for capillary hysteresis and effective stress, confirming its applicability to real field scenarios.

records.title: Development of Multi-Stage Fracturing System and Wellbore Tractor to Enable Zonal Isolation During Stimulation and EGS Operations in Horizontal Wellbores – Third Year Progress Report
records.summary: Abstract This paper is the progress report for the last two years of a three-year DOE funded project aimed at developing and constructing cost-effective hydraulic fracturing tools. These tools are intended to enable zonal isolation for subsurface heat exchange in Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) field research at the Utah-FORGE site. The project has focused on the development of an economic, scalable completion method for EGS using long-reach, horizontal geothermal wells. The use of cemented sleeves allows the casing to serve as both the frac string and the injection/production string with conformance control—a critical advantage over the existing ‘Plug and Perf’ completion methods. This report describes the development and testing of a Wellbore Tractor for use in temperatures up to 225 °C (440 °F) to effectively detect and control flow. The development and testing of the sleeve and tractor required component level testing with separate Seal Drag and Collet Test Fixtures. These fixtures were used to iteratively design and test sleeve seal systems for sealing capabilities and drag forces, as well as a Collet Test Fixture to test ball catch/pass capabilities. Tractor prototype components were tested "dry" and simulated wellbore conditions. Fracture and reservoir modeling were used in the system design process. The tool development was complemented by evaluating the performance of the Utah-FORGE hydraulic fracturing field tests and the published results of the Fervo Project Red geothermal trials at Blue Mountain in Nevada. Results from testing demonstrated the Collet would always "catch" the ball at 8 bbl/min or less and would always "pass" the ball at 11-12 bbl/min. Testing was highly repeatable over four days of testing with no damage to the ball. Nineteen seal drag tests were performed with final, repeatable drag forces of less than 400 lbs. at 440 °F, 2000 psi differential pressure. Tractor components were successfully tested with a flask in 12-hour duty cycles at 225 °C (440°F) wellbore temperature. Final tractor and sleeve designs were completed with fabrication underway for system integration testing (TRL-6) and field testing (TRL-8). Numerical and analytical modeling of field data established the existence of low permeability in the granitoid and high permeability in the induced hydraulic fracture. Economics modeling demonstrated the importance of conformance control to maintain a balanced flow distribution in all hydraulic fractures, magnitude of the flowrates, and surface area of the heat exchange drainage volume. This paper outlines the tools and methods needed to achieve an economic EGS. Specifically, a large subsurface heat exchanger can be constructed with multi-stage fracturing using cemented sleeves with the speed of ‘Plug and Perf’ techniques. Unlike horizontal wells completed with ‘Plug and Perf’, the cemented sleeve and tractor results in highly improved conformance control to equalize heat recovery.

records.title: Development of BOP API Flange Capacity Using Simulation Approach
records.summary: Abstract Flanges commonly selected for use in offshore equipment are based on the designs found in American Petroleum Institute (API) standards and depend on the predicted load during planned operations and capacity of the flange. The flange capacity is derived from standard analysis techniques provided by API Technical Reports 6AF, 6AF1, and 6AF2. It is however possible to conduct analysis to determine the flange capacities using more sophisticated methods to improve the accuracy of the analysis which can potentially lead to deriving higher capacity results that are less conservative. This paper presents a detailed analysis of an API 18-3/4" 15 ksi BX-164 flange capacity at ambient and an elevated temperature of 375°F. It also clarifies stress and leakage criteria and details the discrepancies in analysis methodology and capacity results between API 6AF2 and ourapproach. To calculate the capacity of an API 18-3/4" 15 ksi BX-164 flange, a 180-degree 3D model is created to calculate the detailed load and stress distribution under different combinations of loadsincluding a flange, hub, and gasket. Both flange and hub are modeled with linear elastic material properties while the gasket is modeled with elastic-plastic material properties. For the flange capacity at elevated temperatures, a steady state decoupled thermal analysis is performed first to obtain the temperature gradient and subsequent thermal stress. The material properties are derated due to elevated temperature per API 6MET. An elastic-plastic approach is then employed to calculate the capacity under a series of load combinations of pressure, tension and bending, using the design factors defined in ASME BPVC, Section VIII, Division 2. The analysis result is based on both stress and leakagecriteria to determine the limiting capacity under various load cases. This work presents a capacity chart that shows the relationship between pressure and bending under various tensions at both ambient and elevated temperatures and further clarifies the stress and leakage criteria. Results show that the overall capacity at ambient temperature based on this analysis is significantly higher than published API reports. Additionally, the capacity of the flanged connection at 375°F is reduced when compared to the capacity at ambient temperature. The capacity reduction from elevated temperature is more pronounced at lower pressures. The flange capacity at both ambient and elevated temperatures is governed by bolt stress criteria. As publicly available capacity charts for API 18-3/4" 15 ksi BX-164 flanges calculated using modern finite element approaches are rare, the analysis method presented in this paper defines a process to calculate the flange capacity at elevated temperatures. This approach can potentially lead to deriving higher capacity results that are less conservative which aids in operational and well design decisions.

records.title: Development and Qualification of a High Angle Multi-Frac (HAMF) Completion System for Deepwater Subsea Wells
records.summary: Abstract Deepwater developments in the Gulf of Mexico have historically focused on high kH (∼10,000 – 100,000 md-ft) Miocene reservoirs. Production from a single sand in these prolific reservoirs has been sufficient to justify the high costs of a deepwater well. In the last decade, there have been significant volumes discovered in Upper/Lower Wilcox age reservoirs in the Gulf of Mexico. These new discoveries typically comprise of stacked sets of lower permeability (1 – 20 md) sandstones. Several of these Wilcox discoveries have been successfully developed using cased hole vertical wells and single trip multi-zone frac-pack completion systems. Despite some of the successes, the project economics of vertical fractured wells in the lower Wilcox remains challenging due to low recovery factors (8 – 20%) and low EUR/layer. This paper describes an alternative lower completion concept for developing these lower Wilcox reservoirs referred to as a High Angle Multi Fractured (HAMF) well design concept. The value of the HAMF concept was assessed via reservoir modeling to understand it's value for low mobility reservoirs. Supporting evidence on the EUR uplift from analogue field studies and analytical modeling is also shown. Functional specifications for the completion system and the frac sleeve were developed based on the reservoir and operational requirements for subsea installations. Following design reviews, a completion system was selected that met the requirements, albeit with some modifications. The selected sleeve system was designed, manufactured, and went through comprehensive qualification and testing. A horizontal cemented 10 sleeve system was installed and hydraulically fractured in a land trial to evaluate the system functionality. Diagnostic evaluation including downhole gauges, radio-active tracers and 3D acoustic imaging are presented.

records.title: Development and Evaluation of an Alternative Fluid for Offshore Fracturing of Moderate to High Permeability Formations
records.summary: Abstract For decades, borate crosslinked guars have been the workhorse for fracturing conventional and higher permeability formations particularly in offshore operations. The development of shales/unconventional reservoirs has led to many new learnings and innovations including new fracturing fluids. In shales, uncrosslinked polyacrylamides (PAs) at low gel concentrations (0.5-2.0 gpt) have become the dominant fluid because of their lower cost, greater friction reduction, and higher retained conductivity. The use of these fluids is commonly regarded to be limited to unconventional formations where permeabilities are in the nano-micro darcy range. Recently, some conventional low permeability (0.1-1 mD) reservoirs have been fractured using higher concentrations (4-12 gpt) of PA in place of crosslinked gels with encouraging results. The potential of these fluids for fracturing of even higher permeability formations (10-1000 md), as commonly found offshore, has not been investigated. This paper describes the identification and evaluation of a linear polyacrylamide (PA) fluid designed to meet the technical specifications for fracturing deepwater/offshore wells in higher permeability formations. Early evaluation identified that a very high polymer loading of 40 gallons per thousand(gpt) would be needed to meet the challenging requirements for offshore application. The evaluation of a 40 gpt polyacrylamides for use as a fracturing fluid has not been looked at by the industry. The qualification and testing program evaluated fluid compatibility, rheology, proppant conductivity, regain permeability, fluid loss, and fluid friction in comparison to a typical 35 pounds per 1000 gallons (lbm/Mgal) borate crosslinked (XL) gel. The practicality of pumping the PA system was also evaluated by an SIT test from an offshore stimulation vessel. The results show that the 40 gpt PA fluid appears to be an attractive alternative to borate crosslinked fluids for offshore fracturing. Its benefits include higher fracture conductivity for improved productivity, reduced formation damage, lower friction pressures, and simpler QC with fewer additives. In some cases, these fluids could replace high density XL-based fracturing fluids needed for fracturing over pressured reservoirs. The SIT test confirmed its feasibility for use in offshore fracture operations.

records.title: Development and Application of HUST: A Hydrogen Underground Storage Screening and Ranking Tool Incorporating Operational Considerations, Geochemical and Microbial Reactions
records.summary: Abstract Several attempts have been made to develop site selection criteria for underground hydrogen storage (UHS) in porous media (UHS-PM). Existing site selection criteria do not consider geochemical reactions and microbial interactions, which are critical processes in UHS-PM. The objective of this work is to share the development of a comprehensive UHS-PM site selection tool and its application in the Sacramento Basin. This work involved building an innovative open-source tool to optimize UHS site selection operations of the saline aquifers for subsurface hydrogen storage. This tool works on the principle of multi-stage screening based on UHS's hydrodynamics, operational, geochemical, and microbial perspectives. The multi-stage screening takes place in three stages. Stage 1 considers the productivity index as the main output and identifies the most important variables affecting hydrogen recovery. Stage 2 is built upon the screening criterion developed from the literature by identifying the conditions that lead to the losses of the injected hydrogen through geochemical reactions. Stage 3 is based on processes that could lead to losses based on the possible presence of microbes. The workflow also has the option to consider the weightage of each physical process, which leads to a more rigorous approach to UHS site selection. The site selection was applied to saline aquifers in Sacramento Basin. Results showed that applying only hydrodynamic considerations could lead to the wrong choice of a storage site because such a site, even with high permeability and porosity, could lead to losses due to geochemical reactions and microbial interactions. By including the weighting factors and reactions, the site that ranked highest was one that could allow sufficient storage of hydrogen, have a reasonable productivity index, while minimizing loss due to geochemical and microbial reactions. The novelty of this work lies in developing a site selection approach that considers the geochemical and microbial interactions when ranking sites for UHS. Such a workflow will close a significant gap in site selection because geochemical and microbial reactions are essential aspects of UHS-PM.

records.title: Developing a Novel Machine Learning-Based Petrophysical Rock Typing (PRT) Classification: Applied on Heterogenous Carbonate Reservoirs
records.summary: Abstract Petrophysical Rock Typing (PRT) from core and well log data is a valuable tool for reservoir discrimination and recoverable reserve estimation in heterogeneous multimodal pore carbonate systems. However, the traditional PRT methods are often ineffective in these systems because of the complex pore geometry and distribution. This work introduces an innovative PRT technique that utilizes cutting-edge machine learning algorithms to categorize petrophysical rock types in a supergiant oil and gas field located in southern Iraq. The study initially employs Ward's hierarchical clustering method to define PRT from mercury injection capillary pressure (MICP) data. Ward's algorithm methodology discovers five separate groups, each of which corresponds to a different petrophysical rock type with a distinct pore geometry and system. The probabilistic neural network (PNN) approach is then used to classify PRTs from well-logging data in a cored well. The PNN algorithm is able to learn the non-linear complex relationships between well logging data and characterized PRTs, and it is able to predict PRTs with high accuracy. The confusion matrix and the total correct percent (TCP) were used as additional criteria to analyze the effectiveness of the PNN classification algorithm's performance. The study's results showed that the predicted and observed PRT had an exceptional match by attaining 94% of TCP based on the testing subset and 95 % of TCP for the entire dataset. The predicted PRT distribution is utilized as an extra independent variable to improve the modelling and prediction of core permeability and saturation height function that are essential to achieve a realistic geological distribution. The study's findings demonstrate that the suggested PRT approach can accurately categorize PRT in heterogeneous multimodal pore carbonate systems. The strategy can be easily applied to different reservoirs and has the potential to enhance the overall reservoir characterization.

records.title: Determination of Production Potentials of Geothermal Resources for Rapid Exploration and Development Decisions
records.summary: Abstract This paper presents a semi-analytical wellbore heat flow model coupled with a formation heat conduction model for rapidly determining output potentials of thermal energy from the open-loop and closed-loop geothermal systems. Energy conservation equations are used to simulate thermal flow dynamics of fluids inside the wellbore, while heat diffusion equations govern the transient heat transfer in the formation. A semi-analytical technique is used to solve these coupled equations iteratively. Model validation was done by comparing the semi-analytical solution with numerical simulation results on a 3D wellbore model for a coaxial closed-loop geothermal system. Good agreement of the temperature profile along the wellbore was observed between the semi-analytical and numerical results. Production potentials of thermal energy depend on the geothermal systems selected to extract the heat from the reservoir. Closed-loop systems rely on the circulation of a working fluid to absorb and transport heat to the surface. Their heat extract efficiency depends on the mass flow rate and initial injection temperature of the working fluid. The higher flow rate leads to a lower fluid temperature but a higher thermal energy output at the wellhead. As the injection fluid temperature increases, the energy output decreases but the output fluid temperature increases. Open-loop systems produce the hot reservoir fluid directly to the surface, in which an increase in the flow rate would increase the fluid temperature and thermal energy production at the wellhead. As the production continues, thermal energy output decreases faster at the beginning and reaches a plateau in the long run. Compared to numerical models, the semi-analytical requires minimal inputs to generate the compatible outputs with higher computational efficiency, which is preferred in many applications, in particular for energy resource screen analyses of new geothermal prospects or repurposed oil and gas wells.

records.title: Determination of Dispersion Coefficient of Solvent in Heavy Oil/Bitumen Under Reservoir Conditions
records.summary: Abstract In this work, the dispersion coefficient of solvent in heavy oil/bitumen is innovatively determined by employing an inverse approach to accurately reproduce the measured temperature, pressure, and production profiles in a heated vapour extraction (H-VAPEX) process, thereby significantly advancing our insights into the dispersion physics under reservoir conditions. Monitoring and surveillance data, including temperature profiles, solvent injection rates, and fluid production rates, from a large three-dimensional (3D) physical experiment for an H-VAPEX test have been meticulously collected, analyzed, and processed. More specifically, the evolving geometries of the solvent chamber have been precisely delineated by integrating the advection-dispersion equation (ADE) with a modified Peng-Robinson equation of state (PR EOS), where the solvent chamber interface (SCI) is theoretically formulated as a function of temperature and solvent concentration gradient. As dispersion physics significantly impacts the SCI advancement, the dispersion coefficient in the presence of porous media can be inversely determined by assimilating the measured and calculated morphological contours of the solvent chamber. Such an integrated model has been rigorously validated with the measured temperature profile of a steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) process from a one-dimensional (1D) physical model collected from literature, and subsequently extended to a large-scale 3D application. In addition, sensitivity analysis has been performed to analyze and identify the key parameters dominating the H-VAPEX performance. Not only does the injection velocity of solvent and its concentration gradient at the SCI exert a significant influence on its anisotropic dispersion in various spatial dimensions, but also the injection velocity dictates the solvent propagation over time. A higher injection velocity is found to accelerate the expansion of solvent chamber, thereby promoting solvent dispersion and resulting in a more pronounced solvent concentration gradient beyond the SCI. Under reservoir conditions and with high injection velocities, the dispersion coefficient is found to substantially exceed the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude. Nevertheless, a large reduction in the viscosity of heavy oil/bitumen saturated with solvent results in a great increase in fluid mobility, facilitating the solvent injection as well as SCI propagation. Through the repeatable and consistent H-VAPEX experiments within the large 3D physical model, this systematic and robust method enables us, for the first time, to not only inversely determine the dispersion coefficient of solvent under reservoir conditions, but also to accurately evaluate and optimize the growth and propagation dynamics of the solvent chamber.

records.title: Detection of Low Contrast, Low Resistivity Pay (lclr) Challenge in Shaly Sand Gas Reservoir Through Acoustic Data in the on Shore Nile Delta, Egypt
records.summary: Abstract In the onshore Nile Delta gas fields, the Upper Miocene Abu Madi clastic reservoir show significant challenges for effective gas production, development, and exploration. The Abu Madi Formation contain unconventional reservoirs, including thin-bedded intervals and low resistivity zones, which are usually overlooked by normal petrophysical evaluation techniques and conventional logging tool analyses. These challenges are mostly clear in areas with significant facies changes, typical of the complex depositional environment of the Nile Delta, or in exploratory wells. Detecting these hidden Abu Madi reservoirs is difficult due to their high shale content, which complicates formation evaluation. The maximum deep resistivity reading in these wet sand reservoirs can reach up to 1.6 ohm.m., while pay intervals exhibit low resistivity readings of less than 2.58 ohm.m. due to high water content. This narrow resistivity range often leads to misinterpretations and affects the pay calculations, reducing the reserve estimation for the whole field. The volume, distribution, and type of clay minerals present in the shale significantly affect the readings which come from conventional logging tools, especially resistivity reading. The conductive nature of clay can mask high resistivity values indicative of gas-bearing intervals, especially when these intervals are thinner than the vertical resolution of the conventional resistivity tools. This study explains that combining conventional logging data (such as gamma ray, resistivity, density, and neutron data) with acoustic data (such as shear and compressional sonic data) can effectively detect these hidden pay reservoirs. This integrated approach depends on the theory that says, while the compressional sonic waves are influenced by reservoir fluids, the shear waves are not affected by it. This methodology helps to mitigate the masking effects of shale conductivity and establishes a strong framework for detecting these hidden reservoirs. Identifying and analyzing these hidden pay zones can significantly increase commercial reserves and production, which is necessary for maintaining low water cut values and ensuring the long-term production of these gas fields. This integrated assessment ensures that valuable resources within low resistivity and thin-bedded intervals are not overlooked, thereby enhancing the identification and understanding of various unconventional reservoirs, including tight formations and shaly sand.

records.title: Deploying Downhole Compression Technology to Enhance Gas Production and Reserves in Mature US Gas Field
records.summary: Abstract In order to unlock the untapped natural gas potential in the United States, it is crucial to implement innovative solutions. This paper focuses on the challenges associated with increasing gas production and extracting liquids from wells with high liquid content. It provides an overview of the process for gathering reliable data from below the ground, explains the main components of the Subsurface Compressor System (SCS), and showcases the results of using this system to rejuvenate an underperforming well. The paper addresses the challenges of gas production and liquid removal, with a particular focus on collecting downhole data, SCS components, and practical outcomes. Innovative instruments and simulations of multiphase flow were used to determine the best depth for the compressor setting. Specialized pressure tests were conducted to validate the system's capacity to deliver, confirming the necessity for a tailored compressor design.

records.title: Deploy Distributed Real-Time Data Pipelines Across Cloud and Edge to Process Rig Data for Easy Data Fusion and Processing
records.summary: Abstract The need for the distributed real-time data pipeline arises from the requirement to process disparate, asynchronous data streams that emanate from edge devices deployed to remote field locations, like drilling rigs, and in the cloud. These data streams need to be combined in real-time to serve advanced analytics applications like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital twins. Because of its distributed nature, this data pipeline not only needs to process data but also manage deployment, containers, and physical and virtual computing appliances. Due to this complexity, today's distributed real-time data pipelines are nearly all built as custom software solutions, incurring expensive development costs, long development time, and introducing an extensive maintenance burden. This paper presents a new framework that builds the data pipelines as interconnected, graphical functional blocks in a single software user interface. Each functional block can be assigned to execute in multiple remote locations. Furthermore, each functional block can be parametrized to support unique properties of each rig. This architecture makes it significantly simpler and faster to build, deploy and scale distributed real-time data pipelines while accelerating data engineering and data science projects that require high-speed, high-volume, distributed real-time data.

records.title: Demonstration of Seamless Interoperability for Automatic Drilling Management in a Multi-Vendor Context
records.summary: Abstract Drilling operations involve many different companies like the operating company, the drilling contractor, and several service companies. The personnel at the rig site contribute to provide recommended actions to construct the well as smoothly and efficiently as possible. The question is whether it is possible to design an interoperability infrastructure that allows the computer systems of each of these companies to communicate with each other's and to provide a pathway for seamless automation of the drilling process across multiple stakeholders. A group of volunteers from several different companies has worked on defining such an interoperability framework. It is a sub-committee of the SPE Drilling System Automation Technical Section named Drilling and Wells Interoperability Standards (D-WIS). To test the designed D-WIS infrastructure, a demonstration has been organized that has been video streamed live for more than three hours. The objective was to show that multiple external advisory systems could provide inputs during a simulated drilling operation while encountering several hard stringers. The demonstration has been repeated three times to focus on specific subsets of the D-WIS infrastructure at each iteration. For simplicity, the demonstration used a simulation environment with a generic Automated Drilling Control System (ADCS) that implemented minimum automation functionalities such as hoist, rotate, circulate and drill. The demonstration has shown that the drilling process state could be estimated and published in real-time on a drilling data hub. The data hub acts as the central repository where all signals are exchanged, following the blackboard system architecture. This includes real-time signals but also more complex data structure such as capability descriptions of the ADCS functions and planning data for drilling and well operations such as pressure and temperature gradients, BHA and drill string configuration, completions, and trajectory etc. In general, the blackboard utilizes semantic technology to allow any data provider and consumer to interpret the meaning of the exchanged information without involving configuration by humans. Furthermore, a composer application gathers the provided advice and generates the configuration signals to the currently running automated functions on the ADCS. A scheduler oversees the progress of the operation and reacts automatically to unexpected changes of context like when drilling through soft to hard rock, or vice versa. The demonstration showed that the advice generated by multiple external applications developed by several independent companies could be processed and managed to control the simulated drilling operation smoothly even though several unexpected drilling situations were generated by the drilling simulator. This demonstration shows that the generic D-WIS infrastructure can play an important role in facilitating the adoption of drilling automation as it allows to develop new automation functionalities once and deploy them everywhere. Older rigs may become "smarter" by retro fitting the D-WIS structure and may become capable of lower levels of autonomous operations.

records.title: Deepwater Open Water Work Drilling Optimization
records.summary: Abstract The use of motorized rotary steerable system (RSS) and advanced measurement-while-drilling (MWD) tools optimized the open-water work (OWW) scope of deepwater drilling operations in Guyana. The objective was to improve drilling efficiency, reduce slide mode drilling, and enhance directional control. While similar BHAs had been used in vertical wells in the Gulf of Mexico, their application in the challenging OWW scope in Guyana was a novel endeavor. To overcome the limitations of the standard bottomhole assembly (BHA), a novel approach was adopted, incorporating a 26-in. rotary steerable system, straight mud motor, and advanced MWD for dynamic surveying. Detailed planning and tool selection, including RSS and motor tendencies analysis, were crucial for establishing initial motorized RSS BHA design. Ten out of fourteen planned wells used motorized RSS BHA, while the remaining four employed a motor and gyro due to anticollision concerns. The study involved optimizing BHA configuration, drilling parameters, and survey acquisition processes to enhance performance. The implementation of the motorized RSS along with advanced MWD tools led to significant improvements in deepwater drilling operations in Guyana. A 75% improvement in drilling efficiency was achieved compared to previous conventional drilling assemblies. The use of the motorized RSS BHA design resulted in the elimination of slide mode drilling, enabling directional objectives to be met more effectively. The average 26-in. section drilling time was reduced by 18 to 28 hours per well. This method allowed for better control and reduced borehole tortuosity, ultimately improving well performance. The success of this approach has now become the standard for future OWW campaigns in the region. Apart from the enhancement in drilling efficiency, this case study has not only pinpointed solutions to overcome directional challenges but has also paved the way for the industry to attain higher inclinations in top hole. This achievement, in turn, addresses challenges encountered in intermediate and production sections by facilitating the creation of smoother catenary curves and delivering less tortuous boreholes. The implications extend to the realm of production and completion, providing a foundation for more streamlined processes and improved precision in the installation of production and completion components.

records.title: Deep Learning-Driven Acceleration of Stochastic Gradient Methods for Well Location Optimization Under Uncertainty
records.summary: Abstract We have developed the deep-learning-accelerated-gradient (DLAG) algorithm, a novel solution for well location optimization (WLO) problems that leverages data collected from the explored parameter space to accelerate optimization. During optimization, we collect data to train a deep neural network (NN), creating a map from well-location parameters to the objective function. We utilize the analytical gradient of the NN, resulting in an effective search direction while saving the computational cost associated with stochastic-gradient perturbations. Our method features a novel NN architecture, the Spatial Pairwise Interaction Network (SPINet) with independent and contextual neural pathways (NPs), designed to capture the primary well characteristics, and its complex interactions with the neighboring wells. For the contextual NP, we explore using the popular Attention mechanism and simpler mechanism with weight-sharing Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) layers. To evaluate the architectures, we designed the Bird Ensemble (BE) test problem which resembles the structure of the WLO problem. The comparison between DL architectures reveals that the NP with a weight-sharing mechanism has superior performance in terms of MSE error and gradient accuracy. The weight-sharing structure allows the model to efficiently model relationships with shared parameters while maintaining invariance to input permutations. For the test function, utilizing DLAG drastically improves computational efficiency, reducing the number of function evaluations required to achieve the same level of optimization by one to two orders of magnitude. Following validation of this test problem, we successfully applied our method to optimizing locations of injection and production wells in the Egg reservoir model. To alleviate random artifacts and the inevitable possibility of encountering local minima, we conducted 20 iterations of the WLO problems both with and without DLAG. The results reveal that, on average, our DLAG optimization method is more efficient than the traditional approach. This efficiency gain is particularly impactful for real-world applications where project timelines are tightly constrained.

records.title: Deep Learning Assisted Multi-Objective Optimization of Geological CO2 Storage Under Geomechanical Risks
records.summary: Abstract In geological CO2 storage, designing the optimal well control strategy for CO2 injection to maximize CO2 storage while minimizing the associated geomechanical risks is not trivial. This challenge arises due to pressure buildup, CO2 plume migration, the highly nonlinear nature of geomechanical responses during CO2 injection on rock-fluid interaction, as well as the high computational cost associated with coupled flow-geomechanics simulations. In this paper, we introduce a novel optimization framework to address these challenges. The optimization problem is formulated as follows: maximize total CO2 storage while minimizing geomechanical risks by adjusting the injection well's bottom-hole pressure (BHP) within bounded constraints. The geomechanical risks are primarily driven by injection-induced pressure build-up, which is characterized by the seismic moment. We employ the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) based deep learning model to construct surrogate models, replacing the time-consuming coupled flow-geomechanics simulations for evaluating the objective function. The input features of the FNO-based proxy model comprise flow properties and well controls. Meanwhile, the outputs consist of time-series reservoir pressure and CO2 saturation as the state variables. The FNO-based proxy model is trained on a synthetic case simulating large-scale CO2 storage. The results demonstrate that the deep learning-based proxy models accurately and efficiently predict the designated state variables. The developed proxy models have been incorporated into a multi-objective optimization framework through a Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II) to reduce the computational burden. The proposed optimization framework exhibits significant computational acceleration compared to conventional simulation-based function evaluation strategies. A set of Pareto-optimal solutions of the proposed workflow yields nontrivial optimal decisions, diverging from scenarios where geomechanical risks associated with CO2 injection are disregarded. Our findings reveal that the injection rates may not need to reach their upper bounds to achieve the highest storage capacity when geomechanical risks are considered. This is significant because pushing injection rates too high can induce rock failure and unacceptable levels of micro-seismic and leakage events. Thus, the maximum storage capacity is constrained to maintain the reservoir in an elastic state. The novelty of this work is twofold. First, we demonstrate the importance of incorporating the minimization of the geomechanical risks as an objective function into the CO2 storage optimization workflow to mitigate the potential risk of induced micro-seismicity and CO2 leakage. Second, leveraging the FNO-based proxy model to optimize a real CO2 storage operation represents a new approach.

records.title: Decommissioning Subsea Tie-Back Pipeline with Engineered Gel System in the Norwegian Sector pf the North Sea While Main Facility is Still in Production
records.summary: Abstract As larger fields decline in production, tie-backs from smaller infields provide a viable economic solution to all parties in maintaining overall field production; however, decommissioning these smaller tie-back fields have their challenges where the main facility is still in production, such was the case for this case study in the North Sea. An integrated customized chemical solution allowed the operator to successfully decommissioned the 8″ pipelines while mitigating the risks of production disruptions. The greatest challenge was integrating the pipeline system hydrocarbon displacement topsides at the platform without impacting ongoing production from several other infield producers at the same time, or export quality after subsequent passage through the platform's process system. A crosslinked gel train was the concept selected for the pipeline system decommissioning from subsea to subsea. Due to restriction on subsea connection, the gel would need to be crosslinked subsea prior to entering the pipeline. It would also require breaking before it reached the subsea choke due to subsea pressure limitations and passage into the well. The trial provided two critical points to the overall operation, the flowrate at which the gel could be displaced into the well, and the required concentration and injection rate for the breaker to reduce the fluid viscosity and break the gel prior to entering the well. The breaking time had to occur just prior to reaching the tree choke and more critically prior to entering the well. The scenario was carefully analyzed and planned, making sure the crosslinker was injected subsea downstream of choke valve, while breaker solution was injected prior entering the well at the receiving end. Through using this customized chemical solution, the operator company did not require a diving vessel, pig launcher-receivers, nor oil tankers, neither affecting the platform production and operations, and at the same time creating a considerable economic benefit. Pipelines were decommissioned successfully using a gel system. This paper will discuss how the collaboration and engineering solutions enabled the decision-making process, leading to the successful execution of this special project. It will also outline how chemical solutions add value to even decommissioning operations allowing cost savings and solving the challenges.

records.title: Decision Criterion for Stimulation Method: Proppant Fracturing, Acid Fracturing, or Matrix Acidizing?
records.summary: Abstract Most oil and gas wells are stimulated. In unconventional reservoirs, proppant fracturing is the preferred stimulation technique. However, in higher permeability conventional carbonate reservoirs, matrix acidizing and acid fracturing can also result in stimulated wells, usually with lower risk and cost. This article presents a decision criterion for the preferrable stimulation technique considering a combination of parameters, including permeability, stress, geomechanical properties, mineralogy, injection rate, proppant, fracturing fluid, and acid concentrations and volumes. This article is an extension of a previous study, in which a decision criterion was presented comparing only acid stimulation methods - matrix acidizing and acid fracturing. The present study developed a similar methodology to include proppant hydraulic fracturing in the analysis. The proposed methodology was developed using analytical derivations and validated using numerical simulators for both stimulation operations and production. The results were also validated and adjusted using field results and operational constraints. The final decision criterion is analytical and simple enough to be used in initial phases of conceptual design using a spreadsheet. The developed decision criterion was implemented in a simple software and has been used in conceptual design phase for several projects in offshore Brazil carbonates for a few years. It is especially useful in early conceptual design for two main reasons: (1) in this early stage there is usually not enough information available to justify using more complex and detailed numerical simulators, and (2) the well completions are often defined in this early stage, which requires a predefinition of the stimulation technique. Due to lower cost, risk, and simpler operations, acid stimulation methods are usually preferred when they yield similar results. Matrix acidizing is simpler and less risky than acid fracturing, which in turn is simpler and less risky than proppant fracturing. Agreeing with field observations, the presented calculation method shows that in low confining stress and hard rocks, acid fracturing can yield better results than matrix acidizing. However, acid fracturing is less effective in high permeability, high confining stress, or soft rocks. Proppant fracturing can usually result in more stimulated wells than the acid stimulation techniques in low permeabilities, but not in high permeabilities - despite higher cost and operational risk. This calculation method presents an agile quantitative estimate of the gain in productivity index that can be achieved by each technique, allowing an engineered quantitative decision for the stimulation method and corresponding well completion. It was observed that, although there is a good collection of stimulation models and software available, this simple method and its analytical equations provide insight and agility that cannot be replaced by software.

records.title: Damage Classification of Oil & Gas Equipment Components Using Siamese Networks
records.summary: Abstract Visual inspections are non-destructive testing methods that involve the assessment of a material, component, or product to determine its current condition and maintenance schedule. This is done visually, either unaided or with the assistance of a tool. It serves as the initial check for both new and in-service equipment. The process involves scrutinizing the quality of surfaces to uncover any superficial flaws that may have occurred during production or might develop during operation. Although visual inspection is an integral part of any integrity asset management strategy, current visual inspection workflows are marked by experience-driven rules, based on which one can assign damage severity levels to any type of equipment or component. The evolution of the latest technologies for capturing images (e.g., drones, 360° cameras) has reduced the requirements of physical inspections in the field. However, the number of images captured by these devices in a single iteration is huge (e.g., 100,000+). Manually inspecting these images is a persistent challenge and requires a significant amount of human effort, time, cost, and consistency across the entire process. Hence, the need for an automated visual inspection workflow is paramount. The paper introduces a Siamese network-based damage classification application that enables faster execution of the visual inspection workflow. Siamese networks work by learning the features associated with a class based on differences and similarities between given triplets of images. The methodology has an added advantage over conventional classification approaches in terms of the data required to train the model for different equipment. The embeddings for a pre-defined set of images are generated and stored. Comparison of any unseen image embedding is performed against this set of predefined embeddings. Based on the similarity of the unseen embedding with the existing set, a damage class is assigned to the given image. By reducing the amount of data needed, the methodology enables quick extension of the existing workflow to previously unseen equipment.

records.title: Cyclic Pressure Response of Deformed Casing after Discrete Geomechanically-Driven Shear Displacement in Multi-Fractured Horizontal Wells
records.summary: Geomechanically-driven casing deformation that limits well accessibility is known to occur in certain basins where hydraulic fracturing is employed to stimulate production. Completions teams are often faced with decisions relating to whether the well can still be operated at the original stimulation pressure, and the impact of remedial milling work on pipe capacity. This paper specifically explores the structural response of casing to cyclic pressure loading in situations where local deformation has previously been caused by discrete formation shear movement. Discrete geomechanical shear generally manifests in casing as a combination of centerline offset and local pipe ovality, and can be quantified through appropriately-interpreted geometric logs. These logs can be used as input to numerical analysis work, which can provide estimates of the associated plastic strain distribution and loading state in the deformed tubular and insight into fundamental casing response after the deformation has occurred. Using three-dimensional finite element analysis (FEA) of a typical tubular subjected to a shearing event and subsequent cyclic re-pressurization, a parametric approach is taken to estimate the impact of shear magnitude and axial extent on subsequent local strain development, pipe ovality evolution, and cyclic pressure capacity. Numerical analysis generally indicates modest shear-induced casing deformation will not appreciably reduce the rupture pressure capacity of the casing, provided excessive wall thickness is not lost during milling operations and the casing retains its ductility in the well environment. Consequently, accessibility issues will tend to govern casing functionality before shear deformations compromise its integrity. This does not cover all possible scenarios or preclude the need for diligence in assessing the casing's capacity, and will benefit from appropriate characterization of the deformation before (and preferably after) re-pressurization and after any intervention operations that might compromise integrity. By contrast, industry experience indicates connections can be especially sensitive to shear loads, high local curvature loads, and axial tensile strain, and will generally be less tolerant to re-pressurization without seepage or parting if they are unfavorably located relative to the shear location. While many simplifications and approximations are used in this work, the results provide an initial direction should a more rigorous evaluation basis be required to support completions team decisions. This paper extends prior work by the authors to characterize burst and collapse susceptibility of tubular bodies in post-yield strain-based loading conditions, with the specific objective of assessing the potential need to reduce fracturing pressure for subsequent stages. Initial validation of the analysis results has been obtained by comparison to field experience with well-characterized deformation shapes, and will benefit from more comprehensive study to support confidence in field application.

records.title: Coupled Formation, Wellbore, and Flowline Simulation to Explain Formation Tester Dual-Packer Cleanup
records.summary: Abstract A computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and hydraulic system cosimulation method was implemented to understand formation tester dual-inlet dual-packer cleanup in oil-based mud. The simulation includes miscible multispecies fluids in the formation, the dual-packer interval (sump), and the formation tester flowlines, with the objective of reconciling a long-observed dual-packer discrepancy between simulated and observed formation fluid cleanup and generating operational best practices. A commercial CFD simulator is used to perform coupled simulations for flow in formation rock and in the dual-packer sump. Unlike reservoir simulators, which apply a simplified sandface condition using a well model, the CFD simulator includes the dynamics of fluid flow in the wellbore. Next, a simplified hydraulic tool flowline model is coded using JAVA, and a JAVA scripting functionality within the CFD simulator connects the CFD solver with the hydraulic model. This method includes mud, mud filtrate (filtrate), and reservoir hydrocarbons and honors the full pressure and flow rate history from the reservoir to the tool. Results show that when fluid sampling cleanup is initiated, flow into the dual-packer sump always starts from the top of the interval. This is caused by the pressure gradient difference between the sump (mud) and formation fluid (filtrate and native hydrocarbon). Simulations with a light hydrocarbon formation fluid result in native fluids fingering through the higher-viscosity filtrate. As the sump pressure continues to decrease, fluids start to enter the interval farther down, creating some density-driven flow circulation in the sump, particularly when the pumps are stopped for an early pressure buildup. The sump region below the lower inlet cleans up much more slowly because the heavier mud is not easily displaced with filtrate or hydrocarbon. Cosimulation that includes the flowline adds significant insights. While sump pressure is driven by flow from formation and by the dual-packer interval fluid densities, measured pressure at the tool pressure gauge also depends on the friction loss between the tool inlet and gauge (which is a function of flow rate, valve positions, and flowing fluid viscosity), flowline fluid head, and potential inlet filter restrictions. The method represents the dynamic responses of the system which is used to explain counterintuitive gauge pressure observations and cleanup behavior. Current commercial reservoir simulators routinely model flow through porous media, but they do not include detailed flow behavior in the wellbore section that is isolated by the dual packer. Similarly, hydraulic flow simulators exist, but are not often coupled to the reservoir. The novelty of this cosimulation is the ability to simulate the interactions between the formation rock, the dual-packer interval, and the flowlines, which are used to explain counterintuitive pressure phenomena and dual-packer cleanup.

records.title: Cost-Effective Sealing of Geothermal Wells by Modifying Existing Elastomers
records.summary: Abstract Sealing a geothermal well has been a challenging problem due to high temperatures surrounding the well, which may induce thermal deformation and degradation to the constituent polymer of a seal, impairing the hydraulic integrity of the well and thus reducing the thermal energy production of the well. To address this issue, this study focuses on developing an advanced nano-reinforcement technique to create thermally resistant polymer nanocomposites for sealing geothermal wells. The surface property of graphite nanoplatelets (GNPs) is improved via acid functionalization introducing stable carboxyl (-COOH) groups. Subsequently, polymeric nanocomposites are synthesized by respectively compounding various concentrations, namely 1.5 wt.%, 3.0 wt.%, 6.0 wt.%, and 9.0 wt.%, of modified GNPs with ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM). The compounding method enables GNPs’ dispersion within the EPDM matrix and GNPs’ connection to the matrix. It is found that incorporating 6.0 wt.% of modified GNPs increases the high-temperature storage modulus of EPDM by up to 210.11% and enhances the loss modulus by 156.27%. Compared to pure EPDM, the developed nanocomposites demonstrate superior deformation resistance by effectively dissipating energy. Furthermore, the nanocomposite containing 6.0 wt.% of GNPs possesses noticeably higher thermal stability than pure EPDM. These findings suggest that this prepared nanocomposite holds significant potential as a sealing material for geothermal wells.

records.title: Control Line-Less Casing Valve Installations and Reduction of Drilling Operations Risks in Challenging Well Environments
records.summary: Abstract The pursuit of continuous improvement in overall Health, Safety and Environment (HSE) performance represents a key driver in drilling and completion activities, even more in critical well environments. To minimize risks in subsea well operations, Eni and Weatherford developed an innovative Cable-Less Casing Valve (will be referenced as "Valve" in this paper), with the primary objective of blowout risk reduction, isolating downhole environment from surface when the bottomhole assembly (BHA) is out of the well, enhancing operational efficiency through contactless technologies easier to deploy at greater depths. This technology is the result of a joint R&D project in which a pre-existing technology (i.e., a surface cable activated casing valve) has been upgraded by introducing a contactless activation, thus unlocking the application in subsea wells, the main candidates for this technology. Once the technological needs have been identified, the Valve has been engineered, built and pilot tested in land environment in 2018 - 2019, prior to its commercial deployment occurred in the Eastern Mediterranean Sea area for three subsea wells between 2022 and 2024, achieving the expected objectives with no major interference or disruption added to the normal operations. The Valve has been developed in sizes for 13 3/8″ – 13 5/8″ and for 9 5/8″ – 9 7/8″ casings.

records.title: ConGANergy: A Framework for Engineering Data Augmentation with Application to Solid Particle Erosion
records.summary: ABSTRACT Erosion is a phenomenon involving material removal due to fluid entrained particles impinging on material surfaces. Experiments are crucial to investigate erosion severity and the impact of different physical parameters. However, conducting these experiments is expensive and time-consuming, and collecting high-quality data is challenging due to the small scales of material removal and sensitivity to external environment changes. Over the years, research at the Erosion/Corrosion Research Center (E/CRC) at the University of Tulsa has focused on investigating solid particle erosion in pipelines and fittings. Experiments are conducted using a large-scale boom tower flow loop, and erosion data is collected with high-accuracy, temperature-compensated ultrasonic transducers. This has resulted in more than 200 sets of high-quality experimental data covering various pipe diameters, particle diameters, sand concentrations, and flow velocities. Mining the inherent patterns and physical laws within this data is valuable for guiding future process condition selections and experimental tests. With the existing data covering a wide range of conditions, machine learning methods can be utilized to augment the data, ensuring the newly generated data adheres to physical laws and has similar distributions. Conditional Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks (CWGANs) are a class of machine learning models designed for generating conditioned data. CWGANs can be applied to generate additional training data when the available data is limited, significantly expanding the erosion databank for subsequent mechanistic modeling. This work proposes the Conditional GAN Synergized SPPS model (ConGANergy) framework for engineering data augmentation, which utilizes CWGANs to expand erosion experimental datasets. We conducted experiments to evaluate the performance of the proposed framework by comparing the newly generated data against original experimental data and data obtained through a semi-mechanistic erosion prediction model Sand Production Pipe Saver (SPPS) developed at E/CRC. This approach provides engineers and researchers with a powerful tool to expand databases and build robust mechanistic models, leveraging the inherent patterns within high-quality experimental data while adhering to the physical laws governing erosion phenomena.

records.title: Comprehensive Experimental and Simulation Studies on Capillary Pressure in Unconventional Production and CO2 Sequestration
records.summary: Abstract Capillary pressure measurements on shale and tight core samples have revealed that this parameter can reach hundreds or even thousands of psi at reservoir conditions. A high pressure difference between the fluid phases can significantly affect the multiphase flow in the reservoir, but this parameter is usually neglected in analytical and numerical unconventional reservoir modeling. This study presents a systematic and comprehensive evaluation on the coupled effects of capillary pressure and wettability on unconventional production and CO2 sequestration. Mercury injection capillary pressure (MICP) measurements were performed on hundreds of Permian Basin core samples based on facies-driven selection criteria. Both mercury intrusion (pressurization) and extrusion (depressurization) were recorded for all samples to represent drainage and imbibition processes, respectively. The exhaustive experimental dataset was used to create type drainage-imbibition curves for capillary pressure and relative permeability in six dominant facies in the Permian Basin. Systematic field-scale mechanistic simulations were performed to evaluate the effect of all integrated parameters on oil production and sequestration. Simulation results show that capillary pressure decreases water cut in water-wet formations and increases it in oil-wet reservoirs. In a long-term CO2 sequestration scenario, high displacement pressure in the matrix constrains gas propagation and storage capacity in shale rocks.

records.title: Comparing Open-Source Drill String Models: Establishing Test Cases and Methods
records.summary: Abstract This paper presents a foundational guide for comparing drilling dynamics models, emphasizing the establishment of methodologies rather than just results. We assess two open-source soft-string dynamic models: the distributed, torsional model by Aarsnes and Shor, and the lumped-mass, coupled axial-torsional model by Dixit et al. Both models are evaluated through six progressively complex test cases designed to enhance methodology development for future model comparisons. Despite their different assumptions and mathematical foundations, both models demonstrated similar responses in drill string vibrations and stick-slip behaviors, with minor differences attributed to the use of distinct friction models (Coulomb versus Stribeck). The study also illustrates the benefits of open-source software in drilling dynamics, such as ease of modification and problem-solving speed, highlighting its potential for improving productivity and insights when combined with collaborative efforts from various industries and academic entities. This work lays the groundwork for further research and robust comparisons of drilling dynamics models, enhancing confidence in both open and closed-source models.

records.title: Comparative Analysis of Microbiological Testing Technologies Used in the Energy Industry
records.summary: Abstract Within the energy industry, there are several technologies used to quantify microbiological contamination of fluids and assets. Some of these technologies can also be used to identify or characterize microorganisms of interest. It is important to understand the scope of detection and limitations of individual assays so that accurate, data-driven decisions can be made. Three fluids varying in chemical composition and origin within the energy sector were tested in this study. Serial dilution for detection of acid producing bacteria (APB) and sulfate reducing bacteria (SRB), activity-reaction tests measuring SRB, an assay quantifying bacterial hydrolases, and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) quantification were compared and assessed against molecular microbiological methods (MMM). Data were collected to determine the ease of use, precision, and comparability of the testing technologies to each other. A kill study using organic biocides evaluated the performance of these tests in quantifying changes in the microbiological populations over time. The testing technologies delivered results on the order of minutes (ATP and enzymatic assays) to days (activity-reaction tests and MMM) to weeks (serial dilution). Comparing data from 1stgeneration ATP and the bacterial hydrolase tests to the data generated by the other technologies proved challenging due to the lack of reference standards and equivocal nature of the raw output from those technologies. A relatively high limit of detection was determined for 1st generation ATP technology in fluids where the bioburden was estimated below 104 cells/mL. Interpretation of results in culture-dependent activity-reaction tests was found to be subjective, requiring users to distinguish between visual indicators to estimate bioburden. This was further confounded when testing fluids for industrial uses that have complex mineral content and turbidity. The choice of culture-dependent technology to enumerate SRB resulted in up to 3-log SRB/mL variance compared to other tests. Variable responses of assayed biomolecules to chemical treatment (e.g., biocide) were notable in the kill study, where the choice of testing technology impacted the interpretation of biocide effectiveness. Accurate evaluation of microbiological contamination is essential to operational decision-making in the energy industry. Understanding the strengths and limitations of different testing technologies ensures optimized chemical treatments, reduced costs, and improved environmental outcomes.

records.title: Chemical and Phase Equilibrium Calculations Applied to Dissolution and Precipitation of Multiple Solid Phases
records.summary: Abstract Mineralization stands out as the most reliable method for carbon dioxide (CO2) storage, transforming CO2 into stable carbonate minerals that remain locked away from the atmosphere. This high security has sparked interest in enhancing CO2 mineralization within geological formations. However, effective enhancement demands a robust thermodynamic model that integrates chemical and phase equilibria (CPE). In this paper, we introduce a CPE model built upon the Pitzer activity and Peng-Robinson fugacity models, solving it through Gibbs free energy minimization. The CPE model can model complex systems involving multiple hydrocarbon phases, an aqueous phase, and several solid phases, marking a significant advance in fluid modeling for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technologies. We applied the CPE model to analyze experimental data, particularly the enhanced dissolution of basalt minerals using sodium formate solutions. Our case studies highlight the model's versatility. One case demonstrated the model's capability to represent seven distinct phases, including an oleic, a gaseous, an aqueous, and solid phases, during CO2 injection into a depleted oil reservoir. In another novel application, the CPE model analyzed ligand-promoted basalt dissolution, revealing that metal-formate compounds in the aqueous solution lowered the chemical potentials of dissolved solids, thereby enhancing mineral dissolution. These findings confirm the CPE model's potential to drive forward CO2 mineralization strategies.

records.title: Chasing Remaining Potential in Mature East Nile Delta Development Blocks Using Machine Learning
records.summary: Abstract A growing number of geophysicists and reservoir engineers are being drawn to machine learning due to its many applications in the oil and gas industry, especially in detecting the hydrocarbon accumulations.Direct applications of machine learning currently cover the whole range of tasks related to the interpretation of seismic data, from automatically interpreting faults and horizons to computer-aided seismic well tying, velocity model optimization, geobodies extraction, and seismic facies classification. In this paper, we demonstrate how artificial neural networks can be used to train a computer to identify seismic data and forecast possible gas accumulations as a quick tool for screening remaining potential in development blocks. More than 20 commercial gas accumulations have been discovered in the study area located in Egypt's Nile Deltawith an exploration success rate of more than 60% attributed to most discoveries exhibiting an abnormal AVO seismic behavior. Gas presence in possible prospects was de-risked utilizing traditional pre-stack seismic data analysis and/or seismic facies classification using seismic inversion products. Much time and processing power are required for this work. Machine learning techniques enable a quick and efficient way for screening large volumes of seismic data with astonishing accuracy. Machine learning techniques were employed to enable a quick and efficient way for screening large volumes of seismic data. Training data selection, filtering of the best-discriminating attributes, and monitoring of the learning process were carried out. The neural network was trained on a few examples in the vicinity of wells. The paper shares a successful implementation of a methodology for identifying gas accumulations in mature blocks for the Messinian stratigraphic level, starting from training data selection through filtering of the best-discriminating attributes and monitoring of the learning process until running the predictions. Although the neural network was trained on only a few examples in vicinity of wells, it managed successfully to delineate known accumulations with almost 90% accuracy. The validation of the prediction power increased the belief in the screening outcome of the machine.The newly identified potential gas accumulations were fed into a voxel-based volumetric evaluation workflow to quickly filter out small sub-economic accumulations. The top ranked identified prospects were recommended for further maturation and possible inclusion in future exploration campaigns. The use of artificial neural networks in identifying gas accumulations and screening seismic data is a novel approach. Machine learning techniques offer a quick and efficient solution for analyzing large volumes of seismic data. The successful implementation of this technology in identifying gas accumulations in the mature blocks for the Messinian stratigraphic level is shared in this paper to be used in other areas for identifying potential gas accumulations whenever applicable.

records.title: Characterizing Joint Distribution of Uncertainty Parameters and Production Forecasts Using Gaussian Mixture Model and a Two-Loop Expectation-Maximization Algorithm
records.summary: Abstract Uncertainty quantification of reservoirs with multiple geological concepts and robust optimization are key technologies for oil/gas field development planning, which require properly characterizing joint distribution of model parameters and/or production forecasts after conditioning to historical production data. In this work, an ensemble of conditional realizations is generated by a multi-realization history-matching (MHM) workflow. The posterior probability-density-function (PDF) of model parameters and/or production forecasts is non-Gaussian and we approximate it by a Gaussian-mixture-model (GMM) using an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. This paper first discusses major limitations of the traditional EM algorithm--not robust and converging to suboptimal solutions. We develop a two-loop EM algorithm (EM-EVD-TL) using the compact form of eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) and propose new strategies to overcome these limitations: (1) Reduce the dimension of a Gaussian component if its covariance matrix becomes singular; (2) introduce an inner EM-loop in which only the diagonal matrix in EVD of the covariance matrix is updated. The first strategy improves the stability and convergence of the EM algorithm in dealing with degeneration of Gaussian components. The second strategy reduces the computational cost and further improves the convergence rate. The proposed EM-EVD-TL algorithm was validated on an analytical testing example, and its performance is compared against the single-loop, traditional EM algorithms which use either Cholesky-decomposition (EM-CD) or EVD (EM-EVD). An ensemble of conditional realizations is generated from sampling the actual PDF using the Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC) approach. For the analytical example, the GMMs approximated by three EM algorithms are very close to the actual distribution with negligible difference. Finally, we applied the proposed EM-EVD-TL algorithm to realistic history matching problems with different number of uncertainty parameters and production forecasts. We first generate an ensemble of conditional realizations using either MCMC method or distributed Gauss-Newton (DGN) optimization method. Then, we construct GMMs using different EM algorithms by fitting the conditional realizations, starting from different initial configurations and settings. Our numerical results confirm that the proposed EM-EVD and EM-EVD-TL algorithms performs robustly. In contrast, the traditional EM-CD algorithm without regularization fails to converge for most testing cases. The EM-EVD-TL algorithm converges faster to better solutions than the EM-CD algorithm. The proposed two-loop EM-EVD-TL algorithm has many potential applications and thus helps make better decisions: (1) Close gaps between theoretical formulations of history matching and real applications; (2) characterize posterior distribution of reservoir models having multiple geological concepts or categories; (3) select high-quality P10-P50-P90 representative models; (4) reparametrize gridblock-based properties; and (5) conduct robust well-location and well-control optimization (WLO/WCO) under uncertainty, e.g., through seamless integration of EM-GMM with our advanced multi-objective optimization techniques.

records.title: Characterizing Acoustic-Based Reservoir Injectivity Monitoring with Perforation Laboratory Testing
records.summary: Abstract This paper investigates the application of a laboratory experiment to acoustically characterize and monitor carbon dioxide (CO2) injection at the scale of the perforation interval. We perform a perforating laboratory experiment to replicate the flow of supercritical fluid through a perforated casing into a permeable rock formation at reservoir conditions, mimicking carbon dioxide (CO2) injection typical of carbon capture and storage (CCS) operations. We capture acoustic signals during controlled flow experiments at various injection pressures with a hydrophone. Analysis of the spectral content revealed distinct characteristics in the specific acoustic bands, indicating the potential for passive acoustic monitoring to quantify injection processes. In practice, that permanent monitoring would be achieved via distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). We acknowledge the need for further research and development to subsequently derive an equivalent DAS response for quantifying CO2 injection rates at the individual perforation level to improve understanding of CO2 injectivity.

records.title: Characterization of Cement’s Temporal Mechanical Properties Under Simulated Downhole Conditions
records.summary: Abstract The evolution of cement mechanical properties is crucial for the performance of zonal isolation and determining the wait-on-cement period. To address this, a triaxial testing facility is developed that directly measures cement static elastic modulus and Poisson’s ratio of cement under in situ conditions. The accuracy of this facility was validated by measuring the bulk modulus of water. To obtain the temporal evolution of cement mechanical properties, an unloading-loading cycle every 30 mins was used from the beginning to the end of the experiment. An amplitude of 10 MPa during cyclic loading guarantees that the cement is in the elastic stage. The theory of poroelasticity was applied to estimate cement elastic modulus and Poisson’s ratio. A 7-day experiment was conducted under axial stress cycling between 40 MPa and 30 MPa, with a confining stressof 25 MPa. The Class G Cement, with a water-cement ratio of 0.4,began to gel after curing for 350 minutes (min), with rapid strength growthoccurring between 400 to 2000 min. After this period, the cement’s elastic modulus stabilized between 47 and 55 Gigapascal (GPa), and its Poisson’s ratio reached 0.35. These values are significantly higher than those obtained from the conventional triaxial compression tests. Overall, our work provides one way to evaluate cement in situ mechanical properties, which can be highly valuable for geothermal and deepwater drilling applications.

records.title: Capillary Dynamics of Nanoconfined Water and CO2 Induced by Time-Dependent Wettability Alteration
records.summary: Abstract Formation wettability alteration (WA) is ubiquitous in nature and relevant to many applications spanning from geological CO2 storage to enhanced oil/gas recovery. WA and the induced capillary dynamics are of great significance in caprocks and shale reservoirs. However, the impact of nanoconfinement effect has rarely been studied. In this work, we developed a new dynamic capillary pressure model for nanoconfined water and CO2 considering time-dependent WA. A sorption-based WA model was adopted to describe the variation of wettability over time. Dynamic capillary pressure model was then established by coupling the time-dependent WA model and numerical modelling of H2O-CO2 drainage and imbibition in nanoscale bundle-of-tubes. To adapt to the nanoconfined environment, slip and entrance/exit loss modified Lucas-Washburn flow model was developed by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and interfacial tension (IFT) was predicted using nanoscale-extended Cubic-Plus-Association equation of state and the density gradient theory. Cycles of H2O-CO2 drainage and imbibition were implemented in the nanoscale bundle-of-tubes, until the wettability of all the tubes reached its final state. Based on the results, a quantitative dynamic capillary pressure model was established with a term characterizing the speed and extent of change. The impact of nanoconfinement was investigated, where slip and entrance/exit loss effect accelerated the capillary pressure alteration, while IFT shift due to fluid-wall interaction slowed it down. The influence of pore structure was also examined. The capillary pressure of pores with triangular cross-sections changed fastest, followed by those with square cross- sections, and circular cross-sections; tortuosity reduced the speed of capillary pressure change. This new nanoscale-extended dynamic capillary pressure model accounts for the rock-fluid interaction and long-term WA induced by WA agent adsorption, which are usually ignored by conventional capillary pressure models.

records.title: Calcium Carbonate Risk Index Assessment for Smart Completion Systems Employing Thermodynamic and Kinetic Precipitation Rates
records.summary: The formation and deposition of inorganic salts on industrial equipment surfaces pose significant financial and technological challenges for various industries, particularly the oil industry, because of the transportation of multiphase fluids, such as water, oil, and gas, under high temperature, pressure, and salinity conditions (Crabtree et al., 1999; Kamal et al., 2018). Calcium carbonate scaling presents a particular challenge for scale control, as it is sensitive to pressure and temperature variations (Blue et al., 2017; Cosmo, 2013a; Du & Amstad, 2019). Smart completions are a favored method for production control and scale surveillance, as they enable the reduction of water production or the mixing of incompatible water chemistries (Bouamra et al., 2020; Santos et al., 2017). However, the design, size, and geometry of smart completion tools can impact the prevention of scaling deposition. Thus, there is a need to investigate operating conditions and equipment designs that can influence the formation and deposition of precipitates within the oil production process (Lai et al., 2020; Olajire, 2015). A mathematical methodology has been developed to predict precipitation rates along the oil and gas workflow within these smart completions. This involves a comprehensive simulation of the particles, characterizing the kinetic, thermodynamic, and fluid-dynamic aspects of CaCO3 produced within the fluids in the oil and gas industry.
